summary:
No Rize-specific measure, enforcement programme or institution concerning transgender visitors is documented in the sourced material. A trans visitor to Rize Province stands under Turkey's national framework in full: the province applies Turkish law and Turkish policing practice, and the findings below are the national picture that a visitor crosses into.

That framework has moved toward criminalisation without the prohibitions yet being on the books. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked 11th Judicial Reform package would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people, calling it one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against its provisions. Amnesty International's Türkiye country report for 2025/26 records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025, an assault that would criminalise any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible to obtain. None of the three was submitted to parliament.

The legislative position shifted again in 2026. The discriminatory LGBTI provisions of the draft judicial package were removed, and a February 2026 press report described a separate proposed law criminalising publicly encouraging "behaviour contrary to biological sex" with one to three years in prison; that proposal was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill, the 12th judicial package. A visitor therefore faces a regime in which prohibitions are proposed, dropped and re-proposed within months, while street-level enforcement continues on the strength of administrative and discretionary powers rather than a new statute.

The baseline law is comparatively permissive on its face. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. There is, however, no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised. The absence of a discrimination statute removes the ordinary route by which a visitor or resident would challenge differential treatment by police, hotels, clinics or transport operators.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service. Conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a "psychosexual illness", must provide photographic proof of their claims, and risk their "unfit report" leaking publicly. This affects Turkish citizens rather than visitors, but it evidences the official classification of queer identity as pathology that shapes how state institutions treat gender variance generally.

Pride events remain the most visible flashpoint. Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans. In June 2025 the authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images on social media incompatible with "society's moral values" and that it could "encourage or promote" LGBTI identities.

Transition-related care is tightening. In June 2025 the Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency, under the Ministry of Health, banned the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21. A visitor who depends on uninterrupted hormone supply should treat Turkish pharmacies as an unreliable source for anyone under that threshold, and should carry an adequate personal supply with documentation.

Checkpoint practice is the sharpest document risk. Under the national framework, Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in 2025 in Beyoğlu streets, shops and cafés and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release; legal experts cited argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and one detainee recorded that no fine was issued but she was documented anyway, with the unpassed law already being applied to her. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is thus an occasion on which a passport is compared against presentation, and a mismatch is a direct outing risk.

The broader record indicates that hostility is a documented state posture rather than residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 through formal channels and 43 off the record. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected. Monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.
tangentialFactors:
The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Rize, on Turkey's Black Sea coast, sits in a socially conservative region where that framing is unlikely to be countered by local counter-messaging, but the sourced material records no Rize-specific mobilisation, protest or official statement in either direction.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

The historical depth of the pattern predates the current legislative cycle. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

Documented deterioration across the period is measurable rather than impressionistic: three draft packages in 2025, a hormonal prescribing ban in June 2025, blanket Pride bans with mass detentions in June 2025, an association dissolved in December 2025, and the Sincan Women's Prison death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz on 1 December 2025, which opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised in parliament on 12 December 2025. The counter-current — removal of the discriminatory provisions in 2026 and the omission of the February 2026 proposal from the omnibus bill — shows legislative outcomes remaining unsettled while administrative measures hold.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition has been available to Turkish citizens since 1988, but Amnesty International's 2025/26 reporting notes that the draft packages would have made it nearly impossible to obtain, and the current route is under active political pressure.

Residents face the June 2025 Ministry of Health agency ban on prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21, alongside a Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 — following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports — barring hospitals from recording the "other" option and requiring e-reports to be issued, which risks profiling trans patients in official records.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities: a transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and the case confirmed in parliament that a trans man had been held in a women's prison. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, a binary and heteronormative administration, transfers that frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints processes that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Openly LGBTQ Turkish citizens are barred from military service under a classification of homosexuality as a "psychosexual illness", with photographic proof required and an "unfit report" at risk of public leakage. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and there is no comprehensive anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Rize-specific source in the inventory addresses policing, hospitals, hostels or ID checks in Rize itself. Whether Rize police conduct GBT stops of the type documented in Istanbul, and whether Rize accommodation or clinics apply discretionary refusals, is unresolved on the available material; the dossier rests on the national framework extending to the province.

Whether the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation and the June 2025 under-21 hormone ban are applied by Rize's public hospitals is not sourced. The Kayseri circular cited is a provincial instrument from a different region, cited as the reported antecedent to the national rule rather than as evidence about Rize facilities.

The legislative position is genuinely unsettled rather than closed: the three 2025 packages were not submitted to parliament, the discriminatory provisions were removed from the 2026 judicial package, and the February 2026 proposal on publicly encouraging "behaviour contrary to biological sex" was reported in the press and then left out of the 12th omnibus bill. Which measure, if any, is reintroduced is unresolved.

Figures for detentions, prosecutions and violence are national or Istanbul-based; no equivalent annual count for Rize or the Black Sea region appears in the inventory, so the province's own enforcement volume cannot be stated.
